4747.prule: Fixed final (rightmost) full stress, quantity-insensitive, stated as a reduction rule: every non-final syllable of a polysyllabic morpheme is stress-reduced (p.73), the first element of a compound or reduplicate is stress-reduced (p.72), and non-fully stressed syllables in a close-knit phrase precede the fully stressed one (p.70); only the final syllable is fully stressed and carries a canonical tone. Two degrees of reduction: first degree (vowel quality kept, length distinctions neutralised, sandhi tone o-s); second/extreme degree (final consonant lost, vowel -> [ə] = short /a/, all tonal distinctions lost = neutral tone/'architoneme'), the latter applying to Malay-loan syllables with SatM /ə/, which never occurs in final syllables (p.72). The /ə/ condition governs the DEGREE of reduction only, so placement is computable from syllable count. Every fully stressed syllable also bears one of five tentative tone phonemes (p.71, the tentative arrangement of the etic tones of Table III into phonemes) and stress is non-contrastive (Diller 1989 p.4). Court never writes 'stress falls on the final syllable'; the rule is the complement of the reduction statement, formulated over the polysyllabic morpheme, the compound/reduplicate and the close-knit phrase alike (domain word and phrase together), exactly as the catalog codes Central Thai (thai1261, Noss 1964: 'the last syllable in the phrase has at least normal stress', fixed-dominant final, domain 'word and phrase together', not strict).
4747.srule: None described: 'Non-final syllables in polysyllabic morphemes are subject to stress reduction' -- only the final syllable of a polysyllabic morpheme (and of a compound, reduplicate or close-knit phrase) is fully stressed; non-final syllables are reduced in two degrees set by the vowel (first degree: full vowel kept, sandhi tone; second degree: /ə/ syllables, neutral tone), not by position. Court uses no term 'secondary stress'.

4748.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. The source characterises Miao as a whole as a syllable-tone language (every syllable carries a tone that distinguishes meaning; tone system of the same type as Chinese) and on p.105 places the Southwestern vernacular of the Huishui sub-dialect (c. 40,000 speakers; Yashui, Sandu, Doudi, Duanshan in Huishui County; Baitang, Zhongguo in Changshun County) inside that language. Translation of p.3: 'Miao has the general characteristics of Sino-Tibetan languages: 1. every syllable has a tone, and this tone distinguishes it in meaning from other syllables with the same initial and final; 2. the combination of sounds is rather restricted, e.g. only certain consonants may stand at the end of a syllable; 3. almost every syllable has lexical or grammatical meaning; polysyllabic simple words are few. Moreover, the tone system of Miao is entirely of the same kind as that of Chinese.'

4762.prule: Word stress is phonemic (contrastive) and falls on either the penult or the final syllable, with minimal pairs given ('ba:lat 'banana' vs ba'lat 'broth'; '?u:tut 'rat' vs ?u'tut 'flatulence'; man'su:gob 'to quarrel' vs manso'gob 'to burn'). No rule predicts which of the two positions a word takes.

4763.dq: An acute accent (') is used to mark the strongest stress in the word while the circumflex accent (^) is used when the final syllable is stressed and at the same time has a glottal stop.
4763.dloc: Glossary, 'Explanatory Notes', p. 142; glossary entries p. 143, p. 144 and p. 166.
4763.prule: No positional rule is stated. Stress is a lexical property marked word by word in the glossary (acute = the strongest stress in the word; circumflex = final stress plus glottal stop). Both penultimate (ága, áki, áldaw, ámo, áni, bága, bágyo, báhaw) and final (abaká, abó, agóm, akó, amá, anó, apát, bagá, bahá) stress occur, and the glossary contains penult-vs-ultima minimal pairs: bága 'hot coal' vs bagá 'question particle' (vs bagâ 'lung'), sála 'receiving room' vs salâ 'false, error'. Lexically contrastive penult/ultima stress, inferred from the marking practice; the source itself never says 'contrastive' or 'unpredictable'.

4764.prule: Stress is lexically specified within the last two syllables. Davis's convention is that stress is penultimate unless the entry is annotated 'final', and 126 of the 341 entries (37 percent) carry that annotation, on underived roots of every shape (elima 'hand', dalan 'road', likod 'back', mata 'eye', bulan 'moon', dua 'two', lima 'five', ako 'I') and on affixed forms (kumaan/mengaan 'eat', lumuak/mengluak 'plant', lumipak/meglipak 'hit', meneginep 'dream'). No phonological conditioning is stated, and a check of the saved list finds none: final stress occurs both in vowel-final words (12 of 52) and consonant/glottal-final words (112 of 273), and with every penult vowel (a 23/107, e 28/73, i 36/79, u 36/62), so no category is categorically penult or final; there is only a gradient tendency for final stress to be commoner after high penult vowels. Thiessen (1981:10, via Zorc) independently confines word accent in Canipaan and three sister varieties to 'one of the last two syllables of a word' and calls it non-contrastive; Davis's item-by-item marking shows that the choice within that window is a property of the individual word.

4768.dq: One of the findings is that in addition to word-final stress in verbs, manifested primarily in terms of duration, "prominence" in the form of increased pitch is typically also found on one of the earlier syllables in the word. [p.ii] ... I remind the reader that the verb stem is consistently the final syllable of the word. [p.156]
4768.dloc: Abstract p.ii; sec. 2.6 p.27; sec. 2.14 'Verb stem stress and weight' p.51 (p.63); sec. 3.7 pp.141-142; sec. 3.8 p.142; sec. 3.10 p.156; sec. 3.15 'Chapter summary' pp.182-183 (p.194); sec. 5.1 p.254.
4768.heavy: Not a weight-conditioned rule. Gessner's foot analysis makes the stem syllable bimoraic (CVV or CVC, chart (32) p.51) and the stressed stem the heavy member of a light-heavy iamb, but heaviness follows from stem status; placement is not chosen by comparing syllable weights.
4768.prule: Stress, realized as increased vowel duration, falls on the verb-stem syllable (and on the stem syllable of deverbal nouns); it is the head of an obligatory uneven light-heavy iamb aligned with the right edge of the stem. Since the only verbal suffixes are relativizing suffixes, the stem is normally the last syllable of the word. An independent tone system (H phonologically active, culminative, partly lexical) supplies pitch prominence elsewhere in the word; underived mono- and bisyllabic nouns show pitch prominence only, with no durational stress.
4768.srule: None: 'even in words as long as five syllables, there does not seem to be any secondary prominence' (Gessner 2003:140). One durational stress per word, on the stem syllable; the pitch peak on an earlier (prefix) syllable is a culminative H tone that Gessner analyses as independent of stress (see tone note), not a secondary stress.

4768.tone: Gessner analyses Dakelh as a hybrid stress + tone system (pp.182-183, 254): a two-tone system with H phonologically active, culminative (every word has at least one H-toned syllable, with systematic exceptions treated in ch. 4), partly lexical (certain prefixes such as 1st dual subject idud- and future te- carry lexical H), and independent of duration stress; H can fall on the unstressed light syllable of the word-final iamb in bisyllabic verbs. Earlier descriptions differ (reviewed pp.100-105): Morice 1932:7 (Stuart Lake) denies accent beyond a 'slight rest' on the last syllable; Story 1989 (Nak'azdli) posits stress plus pitch accent; Bird 2002 (Lheidli, second-hand via p.105) calls it a stress language with 79 of 111 bisyllables stressed on the first syllable, cued by pitch and amplitude, not duration.

Position is set by morphological structure, not by syllable count or syllable weight (vowel quantity has been neutralized). Rice 1983 (Fort Nelson dialect, nouns only): the system is 'basically one of alternating stress'; as underlined on the page, a possessive prefix is skipped 'for most speakers' and the first vowel after it is stressed (sįní: í only; sɛdɛchinɛ̨: dɛ and nɛ̨, not chi); in trisyllables the first and third vowels are stressed (nímáli; gotthįlɛ), in disyllables both; the suffix vowel is 'often' unstressed phrase-finally (6) and stressed phrase-medially even directly after a stressed vowel (7: kǫtúɛ̨ ts'ɛhtsini, ú and ɛ̨ both underlined), so suffix stress is set by phrase position, not by rhythm. 4770.prule: Fused tone-accent ('tono-acento') system: each word has exactly one accented syllable, and that syllable carries one of three contrastive tone-accent phonemes (high, low, falling), lexically distinctive (minimal pairs kudû 'diablo' / kudù 'piedra', tikí? 'flecha' / tikî? 'hule') with no grammatical function; all other syllables carry non-contrastive, mechanically produced secondary tones; accented vowels are slightly lengthened. The POSITION of the accented syllable within the word is not stated anywhere in the thesis (examples show it on different syllables), so no stress-placement rule is available.
4770.srule: None: one tone-accent per word ('tres fonemas de tono-acento... que pueden recaer, solamente uno de ellos, sobre cada palabra'; 1967: 'One of these and only one is found in each word'); the other syllables are unaccented and carry only non-contrastive secondary tones. 4770.tone: Manrique frames the system as three suprasegmental 'tono-acento' phonemes (alto, bajo, descendente), one and only one per word, phonemic by minimal pairs but without grammatical function (unlike other Pamean languages); unaccented syllables have mechanical secondary tones; accented vowels lengthen slightly (p. 13); phrase melody rises slowly and falls abruptly at the end with no declarative/interrogative difference (p. 17). The 1967 English version calls them 'tone-stress phonemes' (Google Books, p. 334). Berthiaume (2012: 9) reads the Pame descriptions as 'fundamentally a pitch-accent system' and infers, explicitly as his own inference, that stress falls on the lexical root. A pitch-accent reading is thus defensible; either way the source gives no placement rule, hence tone or pitch accent.

4772.tone: Plainly tonal: 'Modern Ixtlan has four different tones on accented final syllables: low, high, rising, falling. On accented penults, there are only three: low, high, falling.' Tone is licensed by the accent: it affects 'the accented syllable and the one following it, if there is one', with five attested two-syllable patterns (low-low, high-low, falling-low, high-high, low-high); rising and falling never occur before glottal stop. The accent itself is only located within the final two syllables ('the last or second last syllable of the word'); p. 229 shows penult accent as the common case in bisyllables ('We have two cases of final accent in bi-syllabic words' against more than sixty cognate sets listed under the eight penult-accent patterns (a)-(h-2)), but no rule, no predictor, and no claim of contrastiveness is given.
